questions.stem: A patient with antiphospholipid syndrome has a prolonged aPTT on routine labs but a history of recurrent venous thrombosis. Which of the following best explains this apparent paradox?
options: Antiphospholipid antibodies interfere with the phospholipid-dependent aPTT assay in vitro without impairing in vivo coagulation
Antiphospholipid antibodies activate protein C, causing bleeding
The lupus anticoagulant directly degrades fibrin in vivo
The patient has a concurrent factor deficiency causing true bleeding risk
explanations: Correct: the 'lupus anticoagulant' is a misnomer; it interferes with the phospholipid-dependent aPTT test in vitro (falsely prolonging it) while the patient is actually hypercoagulable in vivo due to antibody effects on platelets and endothelium.
Incorrect: antiphospholipid antibodies do not activate protein C to cause bleeding; the syndrome is hypercoagulable, and the paradox is a lab measurement issue.
Incorrect: lupus anticoagulant does not degrade fibrin; it interferes with the lab assay.
Incorrect: there is no true factor deficiency in APS; the prolonged aPTT is a laboratory artifact from antibody interference with the phospholipid reagent.
questions.overview: Antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired hypercoagulable state from antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein) causing venous and arterial thrombosis and recurrent pregnancy loss. Despite a prolonged aPTT (a 'misnomer' laboratory artifact from antibody interference with the phospholipid-dependent assay), patients are hypercoagulable in vivo; antibodies also cause false-positive syphilis (RPR/VDRL) testing, and a mixing study fails to correct the prolonged aPTT.

questions.stem: Leucovorin rescue is effective in reversing methotrexate-induced myelosuppression because leucovorin:
options: Is converted to tetrahydrofolate without requiring dihydrofolate reductase
Directly inhibits dihydrofolate reductase more potently than methotrexate
Competitively displaces methotrexate from plasma protein binding sites
explanations: Correct: leucovorin (folinic acid) is converted to tetrahydrofolate (THF) without needing dihydrofolate reductase (the enzyme methotrexate inhibits), bypassing the block and rescuing normal cells' DNA synthesis.
Incorrect: leucovorin does not inhibit DHFR; it bypasses the blocked enzyme entirely.
Incorrect: this is not the described mechanism of leucovorin rescue.
Incorrect: leucovorin's rescue mechanism is metabolic bypass, not enhanced renal clearance of methotrexate.
questions.overview: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking conversion of folate to tetrahydrofolate and thus thymidine synthesis, arresting rapidly dividing cells in S phase. Leucovorin (folinic acid) can be converted directly to THF without requiring dihydrofolate reductase, allowing 'rescue' of normal cells from methotrexate's myelosuppressive and mucositis effects while chemotherapy continues to act on tumor cells.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with pallor and jaundice during a febrile illness. He has a history of chronic mild anemia and splenomegaly, and his mother had a splenectomy for a similar condition. Peripheral smear shows small, round red cells lacking central pallor, and the Coombs test is negative. Which of the following additional findings would most support the diagnosis?
options: Increased osmotic fragility on hypotonic saline testing
Positive ristocetin cofactor assay showing normal aggregation
explanations: Correct: hereditary spherocytosis results from cytoskeletal membrane protein defects (spectrin, ankyrin, band proteins), producing spherocytes that are less deformable and more susceptible to osmotic lysis in hypotonic solution — the basis of the osmotic fragility test.
Incorrect: Heinz bodies indicate oxidized hemoglobin precipitation, characteristic of G6PD deficiency, not hereditary spherocytosis.
Incorrect: the Philadelphia chromosome is the genetic hallmark of CML, unrelated to hereditary spherocytosis.
Incorrect: decreased ADAMTS13 activity is diagnostic of TTP, not hereditary spherocytosis.
Incorrect: ristocetin cofactor testing evaluates vWF function/Bernard-Soulier syndrome, not hereditary spherocytosis.
questions.overview: Hereditary spherocytosis is typically an autosomal dominant disorder of RBC membrane cytoskeletal proteins (spectrin, ankyrin, band proteins), producing spherical, poorly deformable red cells that undergo chronic extravascular hemolysis in the spleen. Diagnosis is supported by a negative Coombs test, increased osmotic fragility, and the EMA binding test; treatment is splenectomy, after which Howell-Jolly bodies appear.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man presents with fatigue and lower back pain. Labs show hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, calcium 11.8 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.4 mg/dL. Skeletal survey shows multiple punched-out lytic lesions in the skull. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal spike, and bone marrow biopsy reveals 25% clonal plasma cells. Which of the following mechanisms best explains his renal dysfunction?
options: Amyloid deposition of serum amyloid A protein in glomeruli
Light chain cast formation obstructing distal tubules
Direct bacterial infection of the renal parenchyma
Osteoclast-mediated hypercalcemia alone, unrelated to light chains
explanations: Incorrect: IgM hyperviscosity is characteristic of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, not multiple myeloma (usually IgG).
Incorrect: serum amyloid A/AA amyloidosis occurs with chronic inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, not the classic light-chain-driven cast nephropathy of multiple myeloma.

Correct: excess free light chains exceed proximal tubular reabsorption capacity, combine with Tamm-Horsfall protein in the distal tubule, and form obstructing casts ('myeloma kidney'/cast nephropathy).
Incorrect: direct bacterial renal infection is not a described mechanism of myeloma-associated renal injury.
Incorrect: hypercalcemia contributes to renal injury via volume contraction and decreased GFR but works together with light chains rather than being unrelated to them.
questions.overview: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell malignancy producing monoclonal immunoglobulin and excess light chains, diagnosed via CRAB criteria (hyperCalcemia, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lesions) plus clonal bone marrow plasma cells. Renal injury classically results from light-chain cast nephropathy in the distal tubule, compounded by hypercalcemia, while lytic 'punched-out' bone lesions result from osteoclast activation via RANKL/IL-6.

questions.stem: Warfarin produces its anticoagulant effect by inhibiting which enzyme?
options: Epoxide reductase, blocking regeneration of active vitamin K
explanations: Incorrect: dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by methotrexate, not warfarin.

Correct: warfarin inhibits hepatic vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing regeneration of the reduced form of vitamin K needed for γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S.
Incorrect: ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited by hydroxyurea, not warfarin.
Incorrect: cyclooxygenase is inhibited by aspirin/NSAIDs, not warfarin.
questions.overview: Warfarin inhibits hepatic vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing regeneration of active (reduced) vitamin K, which is required as a cofactor for γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, plus anticoagulant proteins C and S. Monitoring is via PT/INR (most sensitive to short-half-life factor VII), and warfarin should be avoided in pregnancy due to fetal warfarin syndrome risk.

questions.stem: Compared to anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity, trastuzumab-induced cardiotoxicity is characterized by which of the following?
options: It is typically reversible and not dose-dependent
It is caused by free radical-mediated myocyte necrosis
It shows irreversible myocyte necrosis on biopsy
explanations: Correct: trastuzumab-induced cardiomyopathy (from HER2 blockade in myocytes) is typically not dose-dependent and is often reversible, with biopsy showing no necrosis, unlike anthracycline cardiotoxicity.
Incorrect: free radical-mediated myocyte necrosis describes the anthracycline mechanism, not trastuzumab's.
Incorrect: trastuzumab cardiotoxicity biopsy shows no necrosis, contrasting with irreversible anthracycline damage.
Incorrect: dexrazoxane (an iron chelator) is used to limit anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity, not trastuzumab-induced cardiotoxicity.
questions.overview: Trastuzumab, a monoclonal antibody against HER2, can cause cardiomyopathy (usually asymptomatic decreased LVEF) through blockade of HER2 signaling in myocytes. Unlike anthracycline cardiotoxicity (free-radical-mediated myocyte necrosis, often dose-dependent and irreversible), trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is generally not dose-dependent, often reversible, and biopsy shows no necrosis, allowing re-challenge after LVEF recovery.

questions.stem: Eculizumab and ravulizumab are used to treat paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria by which mechanism?
options: Restoring GPI anchor synthesis on hematopoietic stem cells
Inhibiting complement component C5 to prevent membrane attack complex formation
explanations: Incorrect: PF4-heparin antibody complexes relate to HIT, not PNH.
Incorrect: these drugs do not correct the underlying PIGA gene mutation or restore GPI anchor synthesis; they act downstream on complement.

Correct: eculizumab/ravulizumab are anti-complement antibodies binding C5, preventing its cleavage into C5a/C5b and blocking membrane attack complex formation, protecting against intravascular hemolysis (though extravascular hemolysis from C3 deposition may persist).
Incorrect: ADAMTS13 relates to TTP, not PNH.
questions.overview: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria arises from an acquired PIGA gene mutation in a hematopoietic stem cell, causing loss of GPI-anchored complement-inhibitory proteins (CD55/CD59) on blood cells, leading to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria (classically dark morning urine), thrombosis, and cytopenias. Eculizumab/ravulizumab, anti-C5 monoclonal antibodies, block membrane attack complex formation and reduce intravascular hemolysis, though mild extravascular hemolysis from C3 opsonization may persist.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man receiving cisplatin for testicular cancer develops decreased urine output and a rise in BUN/creatinine after his second cycle. He also reports burning paresthesias in his feet and new hearing difficulty. Which of the following interventions would most likely have reduced his risk of the renal complication?
options: Pre- and post-treatment IV normal saline hydration
explanations: Incorrect: dexrazoxane is an iron chelator used to reduce anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity, not cisplatin nephrotoxicity.
Incorrect: leucovorin rescues normal cells from methotrexate toxicity, not cisplatin.
Incorrect: mesna is used to prevent hemorrhagic cystitis from cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide's acrolein metabolite, unrelated to cisplatin nephrotoxicity.

Correct: cisplatin's dose-limiting nephrotoxicity (AKI) is reduced by IV fluid hydration with normal saline to increase urine output/diuresis; amifostine (a free radical scavenger) is also used in select cases.
Incorrect: fluid restriction would worsen, not prevent, cisplatin nephrotoxicity; hydration/diuresis is protective.
questions.overview: Platinum agents (cisplatin, carboplatin, oxaliplatin) crosslink DNA like alkylating agents and are used for various solid tumors. Cisplatin's dose-limiting toxicity is nephrotoxicity, presenting as AKI, minimized with IV normal saline hydration (and amifostine in select cases); all platinum agents can also cause peripheral sensory neuropathy, ototoxicity, and significant nausea/vomiting.

questions.stem: Bleomycin causes DNA strand breaks and free radical formation, arresting cancer cells in which phase of the cell cycle?
explanations: Incorrect: metaphase arrest describes microtubule inhibitors (taxols, vinca alkaloids), not bleomycin.
Incorrect: DNA damage occurs during S phase, but the arrest point is G2, not S phase itself.
Correct: bleomycin causes DNA damage during S phase, but cells arrest and accumulate/die in G2 phase, unable to progress from G2 to M.
Incorrect: G1 arrest is not the mechanism described for bleomycin.
questions.overview: Bleomycin generates free radicals causing single/double-strand DNA breaks; because this damage occurs during S phase, affected cells arrest and die in G2 phase, unable to progress to mitosis. Its dose-limiting toxicity is pulmonary fibrosis/pneumonitis, particularly in older patients, due to low bleomycin hydrolase activity in lung tissue.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with a painless, enlarging mass in the anterior mediastinum found incidentally on chest x-ray, along with occasional night sweats. Lymph node biopsy shows collagen bands dividing the tissue into nodules, with large binucleate cells found within clear spaces ('lacunar cells'). Which of the following best characterizes the malignant cells in this diagnosis?
options: CD1a+ dendritic cells with Birbeck granules
Cells expressing surface IgM in a starry-sky pattern
CD15+ and CD30+, usually derived from B cells
explanations: Incorrect: CD1a+ cells with Birbeck granules describe Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
Incorrect: a starry-sky pattern with sheet-like malignant B cells describes Burkitt lymphoma, a non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Incorrect: TdT+ lymphoblasts describe ALL, not Hodgkin lymphoma.
Incorrect: CD5+/CD20+ co-expression describes CLL/SLL or mantle cell lymphoma, not Hodgkin lymphoma.

Correct: Reed-Sternberg (and lacunar variant) cells of Hodgkin lymphoma are large, usually B-cell derived, and characteristically CD15+ and CD30+ but typically negative for other B-cell markers; the nodular sclerosing subtype (most common, especially in young women) shows collagen bands and lacunar cell variants.
questions.overview: Hodgkin lymphoma is characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells (large, binucleate 'owl-eyed' cells, usually B-cell derived, CD15+/CD30+) within a background of reactive inflammatory cells. Nodular sclerosing is the most common subtype, often in young women, showing collagen bands and lacunar cell variants, typically presenting with cervical or mediastinal lymphadenopathy and orderly, contiguous nodal spread with generally good prognosis.

questions.stem: A patient with deletion of three of the four alpha-globin genes develops chronic hemolytic anemia. Which abnormal hemoglobin tetramer, composed of excess beta chains, is responsible for red cell damage in this condition?
explanations: Incorrect: HbS results from a beta globin gene point mutation (sickle cell disease), unrelated to alpha gene deletions.
Incorrect: HbC results from a different beta globin point mutation, unrelated to alpha thalassemia.
Incorrect: Hgb Barts (γ4) forms when all four alpha genes are deleted, which is incompatible with life (hydrops fetalis), not the three-gene deletion described.
Correct: deletion of three alpha genes causes HbH disease, where excess unpaired beta chains form unstable HbH (β4) tetramers that damage red cells, causing chronic extravascular hemolysis.
questions.overview: Alpha thalassemia results from deletion of one to four of the four alpha-globin genes, with increasing severity as more genes are deleted. Three-gene deletion (HbH disease) causes excess unstable beta-chain tetramers (HbH) that damage red cells, causing chronic hemolytic anemia with splenomegaly, target cells, and susceptibility to oxidative hemolytic crises, while four-gene deletion (Hgb Barts) is incompatible with life.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with fever, confusion, and petechiae. Labs: Hgb 7.8 g/dL, platelets 18,000/mm³, markedly elevated LDH, undetectable haptoglobin, and creatinine 2.1 mg/dL. Peripheral smear shows schistocytes. PT and PTT are normal. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism?
options: Widespread activation of the coagulation cascade with factor consumption
explanations: Incorrect: Shiga toxin from E. coli O157:H7 causes HUS, typically with bloody diarrhea and AKI rather than the fever and prominent neurologic symptoms seen here.

Correct: the TTP pentad (fever, neurologic symptoms, AKI, thrombocytopenia, MAHA) with normal PT/PTT (no factor consumption) points to TTP, caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, usually from an acquired autoantibody, leading to uncleaved ultra-large vWF multimers and platelet-rich microthrombi.
Incorrect: this describes ITP, which does not cause MAHA/schistocytes or renal failure.
Incorrect: G6PD deficiency causes hemolysis from oxidative stress with Heinz bodies/bite cells, not a thrombotic microangiopathy with this pentad.
Incorrect: this describes DIC, which would show prolonged PT/PTT and low fibrinogen from factor consumption, not present here.
questions.overview: TTP results from severe ADAMTS13 deficiency (usually due to an acquired autoantibody), preventing cleavage of ultra-large vWF multimers, which cause platelet aggregation and microthrombi in small vessels. The classic pentad is fever, neurologic symptoms, acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, and MAHA (schistocytes), with normal PT/PTT distinguishing it from DIC. First-line treatment is plasma exchange; platelet transfusion is contraindicated.

questions.stem: Aspirin is unique among NSAIDs in producing a prolonged antiplatelet effect because it:
options: Irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase for the lifetime of the platelet
explanations: Incorrect: this describes the transient effect of standard NSAIDs, not aspirin's irreversible, prolonged effect.
Incorrect: aspirin inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2, not COX-2 selectively (that describes celecoxib).
Incorrect: P2Y12 receptor blockade describes thienopyridines (clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticlopidine) and ticagrelor, not aspirin.

Correct: aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1 and COX-2, decreasing thromboxane A2 synthesis for the lifetime of the anucleate platelet (7-10 days), unlike other NSAIDs which reversibly inhibit COX and cause only transient platelet inhibition.
questions.overview: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), decreasing thromboxane A2 synthesis and platelet aggregation for the entire 7-10 day lifespan of the affected platelet, distinguishing it from other NSAIDs (which reversibly inhibit COX and cause only transient antiplatelet effects). It is used for secondary prevention of coronary and cerebrovascular events, with adverse effects including GI bleeding/ulcers, tinnitus, and Reye syndrome in children.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is started on unfractionated heparin for DVT treatment following hip surgery. On day 6, his platelet count falls from 220,000 to 90,000/mm³ (>50% drop), and he develops acute lower limb pain with absent pulses concerning for arterial thrombosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Continue heparin at a reduced dose and recheck platelet count in 24 hours
Discontinue heparin and start warfarin immediately as monotherapy
Discontinue heparin and switch to low molecular weight heparin
Administer protamine sulfate and continue heparin at the same dose
explanations: Correct: HIT type II requires immediately stopping all heparin and starting a non-heparin anticoagulant such as a direct thrombin inhibitor (argatroban/bivalirudin), since HIT antibodies drive platelet activation and thrombosis.
Incorrect: continuing heparin at any dose perpetuates PF4-heparin antibody-mediated platelet activation and worsens thrombosis risk; heparin must be stopped entirely.
Incorrect: starting warfarin alone before platelet count recovery risks warfarin-induced skin necrosis from transient protein C depletion in an already prothrombotic state.
Incorrect: LMWH can still cross-react with HIT antibodies and is not a safe substitute; a non-heparin anticoagulant is required.
Incorrect: protamine reverses heparin's anticoagulant effect but does not address the antibody-mediated process, and continuing heparin worsens HIT.
questions.overview: HIT type II is caused by IgG antibodies against heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes, causing platelet activation and paradoxical thrombosis with significant thrombocytopenia (>50% drop) 5-10 days after heparin exposure. Diagnosis uses the 4T score and serotonin release assay. Treatment: stop all heparin, start a direct thrombin inhibitor or factor Xa inhibitor, and delay warfarin until platelets recover to avoid skin necrosis.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin electrophoresis in a patient with beta thalassemia major would most likely show which pattern?
options: Decreased or absent HbA, with increased HbA2 and HbF
Increased HbA with normal HbA2 and HbF
Normal electrophoresis with an isolated increase in HbS
Predominant Hgb Barts with absent HbA
explanations: Correct: beta thalassemia major (homozygous βo/βo or β+/β+ mutations) results in severely reduced beta chain synthesis, leading to decreased/absent HbA (α2β2), with compensatory increases in HbA2 (α2δ2) and HbF (α2γ2).
Incorrect: beta chain synthesis is severely reduced in beta thalassemia major, so HbA would be decreased/absent, not increased.
Incorrect: HbS results from a beta globin point mutation seen in sickle cell disease, not thalassemia, and electrophoresis in thalassemia major is markedly abnormal, not normal.
Incorrect: Hgb Barts (γ4) is seen in the most severe form of alpha thalassemia (four-gene deletion), not beta thalassemia.
questions.overview: Beta thalassemia results from point mutations reducing beta-globin synthesis, most often in patients of Mediterranean heritage. Beta thalassemia major (both genes severely affected) causes severe microcytic, hypochromic hemolytic anemia beginning in infancy as HbF production wanes, with electrophoresis showing decreased/absent HbA and increased HbA2 and HbF; patients become transfusion-dependent with risk of secondary iron overload requiring chelation therapy.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl with known sickle cell disease presents with fever, cough, and chest pain 3 days after being treated for pneumonia. She is tachypneic with hypoxia, and chest x-ray shows a new infiltrate. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Supportive oxygen, fluids, pain control, antibiotics, and transfusion as needed
Observation without intervention since symptoms mirror pneumonia
explanations: Correct: acute chest syndrome, the leading cause of death in adults with sickle cell disease, presents with chest pain/dyspnea/infiltrate, often triggered by infection; management includes fluids, pain control, antibiotics, oxygen, bronchodilators, and transfusion as needed.
Incorrect: splenectomy is not indicated; splenic autoinfarction already occurs in sickle cell disease, and splenectomy is not part of chest syndrome management.
Incorrect: iron chelation addresses chronic transfusion-related iron overload, not this acute presentation.
Incorrect: hydroxyurea is used for chronic prevention of sickling (raises HbF) but is not acute management of chest syndrome.
Incorrect: acute chest syndrome is a medical emergency requiring active intervention given its high mortality risk, not observation.
questions.overview: Acute chest syndrome is a vaso-occlusive crisis of the pulmonary microvasculature in sickle cell disease, often triggered by infection, and is the leading cause of death in adult sickle cell patients. It presents with chest pain, dyspnea, hypoxia, and a new infiltrate resembling pneumonia. Management includes fluids, analgesia, oxygen, bronchodilators, antibiotics, and transfusion as needed to reduce the percentage of HbS.

questions.stem: Which mechanism is responsible for the reduction in hemorrhagic cystitis risk when mesna is co-administered with cyclophosphamide?
options: Mesna binds and inactivates the toxic acrolein metabolite in the urine
Mesna inhibits hepatic P450 bioactivation of cyclophosphamide
Mesna directly stimulates bladder mucosal regeneration
Mesna chelates iron to prevent free radical formation
explanations: Correct: mesna (sodium 2-mercaptoethane sulfonate) binds and inactivates acrolein, the toxic metabolite responsible for hemorrhagic cystitis, directly in the urine.
Incorrect: mesna does not block hepatic bioactivation; cyclophosphamide still requires liver P450 activation to be an effective chemotherapeutic.
Incorrect: mesna does not stimulate mucosal regeneration; it chemically inactivates the toxic metabolite.
Incorrect: iron chelation to reduce free radical damage describes dexrazoxane's mechanism for anthracycline cardiotoxicity, not mesna's mechanism.
questions.overview: Cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide are prodrugs bioactivated by the liver; their toxic metabolite acrolein damages the bladder urothelium, causing hemorrhagic cystitis with hematuria. Mesna binds and inactivates acrolein within the urine, and adequate hydration further reduces this risk.

questions.stem: A patient being treated with rituximab for non-Hodgkin lymphoma should be screened for which infection prior to initiating therapy, given the risk of reactivation?
explanations: Incorrect: toxoplasmosis reactivation is not described as a rituximab-associated risk.
Correct: rituximab (an anti-CD20 antibody causing B-cell depletion) carries a significant risk of hepatitis B reactivation, so antibody screening is recommended prior to treatment.
Incorrect: CMV is not the specifically highlighted reactivation risk for rituximab.
Incorrect: hepatitis A reactivation is not a described risk of rituximab therapy.
questions.overview: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody against CD20 that depletes B cells via ADCC, complement-dependent cytotoxicity, and direct apoptosis, and is used in B-cell malignancies (NHL, CLL), rheumatoid arthritis, and ITP. Its most serious adverse effect is hepatitis B reactivation (requiring pretreatment screening), along with opportunistic infection risks such as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (JC virus) and PJP.

questions.stem: A patient of Mediterranean descent develops acute hemolytic anemia with back pain after taking dapsone for a skin infection. Peripheral smear shows precipitated, denatured hemoglobin within red cells and cells with a bite taken out of the membrane. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible?
explanations: Incorrect: δ-ALA synthase deficiency relates to sideroblastic anemia, not oxidative hemolysis with Heinz bodies/bite cells.

Correct: G6PD deficiency impairs the HMP shunt's generation of NADPH, reducing glutathione's ability to protect against oxidative stress; triggers like dapsone, sulfa drugs, infections, and fava beans precipitate hemolysis with Heinz bodies (denatured Hgb) and bite cells (from splenic macrophage removal).
Incorrect: pyruvate kinase deficiency causes hemolysis due to ATP depletion and rigid RBCs (burr cells), not Heinz bodies/bite cells triggered by oxidative drugs.
Incorrect: adenosine deaminase relates to purine metabolism and hairy cell leukemia drug resistance mechanisms, not this hemolytic presentation.
questions.overview: G6PD deficiency is an X-linked recessive enzymopathy impairing the HMP shunt's production of NADPH, needed to maintain reduced glutathione and protect RBCs from oxidative damage. Hemolytic episodes are triggered by oxidative stressors (infections, sulfa drugs, dapsone, antimalarials, fava beans), producing Heinz bodies (oxidized precipitated hemoglobin) and bite cells (from splenic removal of Heinz bodies), with both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis.

questions.stem: Anti-D immune globulin (RhoGAM) prevents Rh(D) alloimmunization in Rh-negative mothers primarily through which mechanism?
options: Rapid macrophage clearance of fetal D-positive red cells before maternal antibody formation
Direct lysis of fetal red cells via complement activation
Blockade of maternal B-cell receptors for all red cell antigens
Induction of maternal IgM antibody production against the D antigen
explanations: Correct: RhoGAM consists of IgG anti-D antibodies that cause rapid macrophage clearance of fetal D+ red cells from maternal circulation before the mother's own immune system can mount a response and form anti-D antibodies.
Incorrect: the mechanism described in the notes is macrophage clearance, not complement-mediated lysis.
Incorrect: RhoGAM is specific to the D antigen, not a general blockade of all red cell antigen recognition.
Incorrect: RhoGAM prevents maternal antibody formation; it does not induce it, and naturally forming Rh antibodies are IgG, not IgM (unlike ABO antibodies).
questions.overview: In Rh(D)-negative mothers carrying a D-positive fetus, fetal red cells entering maternal circulation (typically at delivery) can trigger maternal IgG anti-D antibody formation, which may cross the placenta and cause hemolytic disease in a subsequent D-positive pregnancy. Anti-D immune globulin (RhoGAM), given prophylactically, causes rapid clearance of fetal D+ cells before maternal antibodies can form, preventing isoimmunization.

questions.stem: A child presents with mucocutaneous bleeding and thrombocytopenia. Peripheral smear shows abnormally large platelets. Ristocetin cofactor testing shows no platelet aggregation even after addition of normal von Willebrand factor. Which glycoprotein is most likely deficient?
explanations: Correct: this describes Bernard-Soulier syndrome, caused by deficiency of the GPIb receptor, which normally binds vWF for platelet adhesion; giant platelets, mild thrombocytopenia, and an abnormal ristocetin assay that fails to correct with added vWF are classic.

Incorrect: GPIIb/IIIa deficiency describes Glanzmann thrombasthenia, which has a normal platelet count and size and a normal ristocetin test but abnormal platelet aggregometry, not the picture described.
Incorrect: 'GPIIa alone' is not a described specific deficiency syndrome.
Incorrect: GPVI is not discussed as a deficiency causing a described platelet disorder.
questions.overview: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder of deficient GPIb receptors, impairing platelet adhesion to von Willebrand factor; it features giant platelets, mild thrombocytopenia, prolonged bleeding time, and an abnormal ristocetin cofactor assay that does not correct with added vWF. This contrasts with Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GPIIb/IIIa deficiency, impaired aggregation, normal platelet count/size, normal ristocetin test but abnormal aggregometry).

questions.stem: The Factor V Leiden mutation causes a hypercoagulable state through which mechanism?
options: Formation of antibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins
Resistance of factor Va to inactivation by activated protein C
explanations: Incorrect: increased prothrombin synthesis describes the prothrombin gene mutation (G20210A), a different inherited thrombophilia.
Incorrect: antiphospholipid antibodies describe antiphospholipid syndrome, an acquired hypercoagulable state, not Factor V Leiden.

Correct: the Factor V Leiden mutation alters the factor V protein so that it is resistant to inactivation by activated protein C ('APC resistance'), allowing factor Va to remain active longer and promote hypercoagulability.
Incorrect: antithrombin III deficiency is a separate inherited thrombophilia unrelated to Factor V Leiden.
questions.overview: Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia, caused by a point mutation in the factor V gene that renders factor Va resistant to inactivation by activated protein C, prolonging its procoagulant activity ('activated protein C resistance'). It is associated with venous thromboembolism and recurrent pregnancy loss, with normal PT, aPTT, and platelet counts, requiring specialized assays for diagnosis.

questions.stem: A patient receiving a vinca alkaloid for lymphoma develops severe constipation, distal extremity weakness, and orthostatic hypotension, while blood counts remain largely preserved. Which drug is most likely responsible?
explanations: Incorrect: etoposide is a topoisomerase II inhibitor causing myelosuppression and nausea/vomiting, not this neurotoxicity pattern.

Incorrect: paclitaxel (a taxane) causes myelosuppression, hypersensitivity reactions, and peripheral neuropathy, but the severe autonomic/motor neurotoxicity described is most characteristic of vincristine.
Incorrect: vinblastine causes severe myelosuppression ('blasts the bone marrow') with milder neurotoxicity, the opposite of the profile described.

Correct: vincristine's classic, dose-limiting toxicity is neurotoxicity (sensory/motor peripheral neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction including constipation/paralytic ileus and orthostatic hypotension) with relatively mild myelosuppression.
questions.overview: Vinca alkaloids (vincristine, vinblastine) bind β-tubulin and inhibit microtubule polymerization, arresting mitosis in metaphase. Vincristine's dose-limiting toxicity is neurotoxicity from loss of axonal transport (sensory/motor neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction), with only mild myelosuppression, whereas vinblastine causes severe myelosuppression with less neurotoxicity.

questions.stem: In a patient with von Willebrand disease, addition of ristocetin to platelet-rich plasma typically results in which finding, and how is it corrected?
options: Normal platelet aggregation regardless of vWF level
Absent platelet aggregation, which corrects with addition of normal vWF
Absent platelet aggregation, which does not correct with addition of normal vWF
explanations: Incorrect: vWD by definition shows abnormal (reduced) ristocetin-induced aggregation reflecting deficient/dysfunctional vWF.

Correct: in vWD, low or dysfunctional vWF fails to trigger ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation, but this defect corrects when normal vWF is added, distinguishing it from Bernard-Soulier syndrome, where the platelet receptor itself is defective and aggregation does not correct.
Incorrect: failure to correct with added vWF is the finding in Bernard-Soulier syndrome (a platelet receptor defect), not von Willebrand disease.
Incorrect: spontaneous aggregation without ristocetin is not a described finding of vWD.
questions.overview: Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by deficient or dysfunctional von Willebrand factor, which normally links platelets to subendothelial collagen (via GPIb) and carries factor VIII. The ristocetin cofactor assay shows absent aggregation that corrects with added normal vWF (distinguishing vWD from Bernard-Soulier syndrome); patients may show prolonged bleeding time and variably prolonged PTT (from low factor VIII), and treatment includes desmopressin to release stored vWF/factor VIII.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with gum bleeding, easy bruising, and oozing from IV catheter sites. Peripheral smear shows abnormal promyelocytes with multiple needle-like cytoplasmic inclusions. Labs show prolonged PT and PTT, low fibrinogen, and elevated D-dimer. Cytogenetic analysis reveals t(15;17). Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment beyond supportive coagulation factor replacement?
explanations: Incorrect: rituximab targets CD20 on B cells, used in B-cell lymphomas/leukemias, not APL, which is a myeloid neoplasm.
Incorrect: hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and is used in myeloproliferative disorders/sickle cell disease, not as primary APL therapy.
Incorrect: imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for CML (BCR-ABL) and GIST (KIT), not APL.

Correct: APL is defined by t(15;17), creating the PML-RARA fusion gene that produces an abnormal retinoic acid receptor blocking promyelocyte maturation; all-trans retinoic acid (a vitamin A derivative) induces maturation of the abnormal cells.
Incorrect: cladribine is a purine analog used preferentially in hairy cell leukemia, not APL.
questions.overview: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (a subtype of AML) is defined by t(15;17), producing the PML-RARA fusion gene that blocks promyelocyte differentiation via an abnormal retinoic acid receptor. Promyelocytes are packed with Auer-rod-containing granules whose release classically triggers DIC (bleeding from IV sites, low fibrinogen, prolonged PT/PTT, elevated D-dimer). Treatment includes all-trans retinoic acid, which induces maturation of the malignant cells.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with a new diagnosis of DVT is started on warfarin monotherapy without bridging anticoagulation. Three days later, she develops painful, dark purple, necrotic skin lesions on her thighs. Which of the following best explains this complication?
options: Excessive inhibition of factor VIII activity
Warfarin-induced antibody formation against platelet factor 4
Direct toxic effect of warfarin on dermal blood vessels
Transient deficiency of protein C exceeding the fall in procoagulant factors
explanations: Incorrect: factor VIII is not vitamin K-dependent and is unaffected by warfarin.
Incorrect: antibody formation against PF4-heparin complexes describes HIT, not warfarin skin necrosis.
Incorrect: this is not the described mechanism; the process results from an imbalance of anticoagulant versus procoagulant factor levels, not direct vascular toxicity.

Correct: protein C has a short half-life similar to factor VII; early in warfarin therapy protein C levels fall faster than procoagulant factors with longer half-lives (II, IX, X), creating a transient hypercoagulable state that causes microthrombosis and skin necrosis, especially with underlying protein C deficiency.
Incorrect: this patient was not on heparin; the mechanism is protein C depletion, not heparin cross-reactivity.
questions.overview: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, blocking γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S. Because protein C (like factor VII) has a short half-life, early warfarin therapy causes a transient hypercoagulable state before the longer-half-life procoagulant factors fall, risking thrombosis — most dramatically as warfarin-induced skin necrosis in patients with protein C deficiency. This is why heparin bridging is used when initiating warfarin for acute thrombosis.

questions.stem: The characteristic 'starry sky' appearance on histology of Burkitt lymphoma results from which underlying process?
options: Deposition of amyloid protein within the germinal center
Collagen bands dividing lymph node tissue into nodules
Reed-Sternberg cells scattered among reactive lymphocytes
Macrophages engulfing apoptotic tumor cells amid sheets of rapidly proliferating malignant B cells
explanations: Incorrect: amyloid deposition is unrelated to the starry sky pattern; this describes amyloidosis, a distinct entity.
Incorrect: collagen bands dividing tissue into nodules describes nodular sclerosing Hodgkin lymphoma, not Burkitt lymphoma.
Incorrect: Reed-Sternberg cells are the hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma, not Burkitt lymphoma.

Correct: Burkitt lymphoma is driven by MYC overexpression (classically from t(8;14)), causing extremely rapid proliferation with a high rate of spontaneous apoptosis; tingible-body macrophages engulfing apoptotic debris create pale 'stars' against the dark 'sky' of densely packed malignant B cells.
questions.overview: Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma driven by MYC gene translocation (classically t(8;14)), causing extreme proliferation rates. Its 'starry sky' histologic appearance results from numerous tingible-body macrophages (pale stars) engulfing apoptotic tumor cell debris amid sheets of densely packed malignant lymphocytes (dark sky); it is strongly associated with EBV infection, especially in the endemic (African, jaw mass) form.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with fatigue. Labs show Hgb 9.5 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, low serum iron, low ferritin, and elevated TIBC/transferrin. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Begin oral iron supplementation without further evaluation
Bone marrow biopsy for ring sideroblasts
Hemoglobin electrophoresis to evaluate for thalassemia
Colonoscopy to evaluate for occult GI bleeding/malignancy
explanations: Incorrect: while iron supplementation is eventual treatment, the source of blood loss must be investigated first in this age group, as untreated malignancy could be missed.

Incorrect: ring sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain are diagnostic of sideroblastic anemia, which shows iron overload (increased ferritin, increased serum iron), not the low iron/ferritin pattern seen here.
Incorrect: thalassemia trait would show a normal or high RBC count with normal iron studies, not the low ferritin/high TIBC pattern diagnostic of iron deficiency seen here.
Incorrect: EPO level assessment is not indicated in classic iron deficiency anemia; it is more relevant in evaluating anemia related to renal disease or polycythemia.
Correct: in an adult or postmenopausal woman, iron deficiency anemia mandates a workup for occult blood loss, most importantly colon cancer.
questions.overview: Iron deficiency anemia is the most common cause of microcytic anemia, characterized by low serum iron, low ferritin (storage form), and elevated transferrin/TIBC (the body's response to seek more iron) with low percent saturation. In an adult or postmenopausal patient, new iron deficiency must prompt evaluation for a source of chronic blood loss, especially colorectal cancer, via colonoscopy.

questions.stem: Unfractionated heparin exerts its anticoagulant effect primarily by which mechanism?
options: Binding antithrombin III and accelerating inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa
explanations: Incorrect: GPIIb/IIIa blockade describes drugs like abciximab, not heparin.
Incorrect: inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase describes warfarin's mechanism.
Correct: heparin is an 'indirect anticoagulant' that binds antithrombin III, greatly accelerating its inactivation of thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa (and IXa, XIa, XIIa).
Incorrect: direct thrombin active-site inhibition describes direct thrombin inhibitors (argatroban, bivalirudin, dabigatran), not heparin.
questions.overview: Unfractionated heparin binds antithrombin III, markedly accelerating its inactivation of thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa, as well as IXa, XIa, and XIIa, and is monitored via aPTT (most sensitive to the intrinsic pathway factors it affects). Its anticoagulant effect can be reversed with protamine sulfate, and it carries risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is found to have marked leukocytosis with a full spectrum of granulocyte precursors, basophilia, and splenomegaly. Cytogenetic testing reveals a 9;22 translocation. Which of the following best describes the molecular consequence of this translocation?
options: Overexpression of cyclin D1 promoting G1-to-S transition
Formation of the BCR-ABL fusion gene encoding a constitutively active tyrosine kinase
Formation of the PML-RARA fusion gene blocking promyelocyte maturation
explanations: Incorrect: cyclin D1 overexpression from t(11;14) is the hallmark of mantle cell lymphoma, not CML.

Correct: the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene encoding a constitutively active tyrosine kinase, driving CML; this is treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors like imatinib.
Incorrect: BCL2 overexpression from t(14;18) is the hallmark of follicular lymphoma, not CML.
Incorrect: PML-RARA from t(15;17) is the hallmark of acute promyelocytic leukemia, not CML.
questions.overview: Chronic myelogenous leukemia is a myeloproliferative disorder driven nearly universally by the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), producing the BCR-ABL fusion tyrosine kinase. It classically presents with marked leukocytosis featuring a full spectrum of granulocyte maturation stages plus basophilia, low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, and splenomegaly; tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib) are first-line therapy, with progression to blast crisis (>20% blasts) representing transformation to acute leukemia.
